questions.prompt: What is another name commonly used in computer science for a trie data structure?

options.text: Prefix tree, because descendant nodes share common prefix string paths.
options.explanation: Tries are called prefix trees because keys sharing prefixes branch from the same parent nodes.

options.text: Suffix heap, because values are sorted by their trailing characters.
options.explanation: Tries do not organize characters as heaps or prioritize suffixes by default.

options.text: Binary bloom filter, because lookups rely on probabilistic bit vectors.
options.explanation: A trie is a deterministic tree, not a probabilistic Bloom filter.

options.text: Indexed ring buffer, because nodes wrap sequentially in circular arrays.
options.explanation: Tries use hierarchical branching paths rather than circular ring buffers.

questions.prompt: What does each node in a standard trie typically store?

options.text: The entire full word string from root to leaf.
options.explanation: Storing full strings on every node wastes memory and duplicates prefix data.

options.text: A dictionary of child nodes and an end of word Boolean flag.
options.explanation: Each node maps outgoing characters to child nodes and marks whether a word finishes there.

options.text: The total count of all prime numbers found in the dictionary.
options.explanation: Tries index characters, not numerical prime attributes.

options.text: A raw pointer to the operating system file allocation table.
options.explanation: Trie nodes live in application heap memory as standard Swift objects.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity to insert a word of length L into a trie?

options.explanation: O(1) is impossible because all L characters must be processed.

options.text: O(N log N)
options.explanation: O(N log N) describes comparison sorting, not trie insertion.

options.text: O(L)
options.explanation: Insertion walks through each of the L characters exactly once, taking O(L) time.

options.text: O(2 to the power L)
options.explanation: Insertion does not branch exponentially; it follows a single linear path of length L.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity to search for a word of length L in a trie containing N total words?

options.text: O(N)
options.explanation: A linear scan takes O(N), but a trie avoids scanning all N words.

options.text: O(N * L)
options.explanation: O(N * L) would scan every character of every word in the dictionary.

options.text: O(log N)
options.explanation: O(log N) is binary search tree lookup, not trie lookup.

options.text: O(L)
options.explanation: Trie search follows L character links, completely independent of the total word count N.

questions.prompt: What is the primary operational difference between the search method and the startsWith method in a trie?

options.text: Search checks isEndOfWord on the final node, while startsWith only verifies path existence.
options.explanation: Search requires that the characters form a registered complete word; startsWith only requires that the prefix path exists.

options.text: StartsWith mutates the trie structure while search leaves nodes unchanged.
options.explanation: Neither query method mutates the trie.

options.text: Search runs in constant time while startsWith runs in exponential time.
options.explanation: Both methods run in time proportional to string length.

options.text: StartsWith converts all characters to lowercase while search requires uppercase letters.
options.explanation: Casing is determined by caller data, not method semantics.

questions.prompt: Why is a trie faster than a hash set for prefix autocomplete in a search bar?

options.text: Hash sets only store numbers and cannot index character strings in Swift.
options.explanation: Swift Set supports any Hashable type including strings.

options.text: A trie walks down prefix characters directly in O(P) time instead of scanning all N entries.
options.explanation: A hash set must inspect every word to check prefixes taking O(N * L) time. A trie jumps directly to the prefix node in O(P) time.

options.text: A trie automatically compresses image assets inside the app bundle.
options.explanation: Tries are text data structures, not image compression tools.

options.text: Hash set hashing operations fail on words with more than ten characters.
options.explanation: Swift hashing works on strings of any length.

questions.prompt: What happens when you insert the words app and apple into an empty trie?

options.text: Two independent disconnected trees are allocated with zero shared memory.
options.explanation: Tries share nodes for common prefix paths.

options.text: The trie throws a runtime exception because duplicate prefixes collide.
options.explanation: Duplicate prefixes are supported by design in a trie.

options.text: They share the first three nodes for a, p, and p, with app marked as an end of word.
options.explanation: Shared characters share nodes; the second p has isEndOfWord true for app, and branches down to l and e for apple.

options.text: The word apple overwrites app and deletes the shorter word.
options.explanation: Both words remain accessible because isEndOfWord flags preserve word boundaries.

questions.prompt: Why should you prefer [Character: TrieNode] over a 26-element array [TrieNode?] in Swift?

options.text: Swift arrays cannot store reference types without explicit pointer casting.
options.explanation: Swift arrays store reference types without issues.

options.text: Dictionaries allocate zero heap memory when empty compared to fixed arrays.
options.explanation: Dictionaries allocate standard container structures.

options.text: Fixed arrays require compiling in legacy Objective-C compatibility mode.
options.explanation: Fixed-size arrays work in pure Swift.

options.text: A dictionary safely supports Unicode letters, accents, and emoji without crashing.
options.explanation: Fixed 26-element arrays assume lowercase ASCII letters a through z and crash when non-ASCII Unicode characters arrive.

questions.prompt: What does the root node of a trie represent?

options.text: The empty string prefix common to all possible words.
options.explanation: The root holds no character value itself and represents the starting empty string prefix.

options.text: The single most frequently searched word in the application.
options.explanation: The root is not a word node; it is the entry anchor.

options.text: The total byte size of all stored characters combined.
options.explanation: The root is a trie node, not an integer byte counter.

options.text: The first character of the English alphabet.
options.explanation: The letter a is a child of the root, not the root itself.

questions.prompt: How can you return all words stored in a trie in alphabetical order?

options.text: By sorting all internal heap addresses in descending numerical memory order.
options.explanation: Memory addresses bear no relationship to alphabetical order.

options.text: By traversing the trie with depth-first search while visiting child keys in sorted character order.
options.explanation: Because prefixes precede suffixes and child branches are sorted alphabetically, in-order DFS produces words in exact alphabetical order.

options.text: By executing breadth-first search across all leaf nodes in parallel batches.
options.explanation: BFS visits by word length rather than lexicographical order.

options.text: By reversing the underlying character dictionaries on every query lookup.
options.explanation: Reversing dictionaries does not generate sorted word sequences.

questions.prompt: When deleting a word from a trie, when is a node safe to remove from memory?

options.text: As soon as the target word has fewer than three letters.
options.explanation: Word length does not govern node pruning safety.

options.text: Whenever its parent node has at least two sibling branches.
options.explanation: Nodes can only be removed if they are not needed by any word.

options.text: When the node has no other children and is not marked as the end of another word.
options.explanation: If a node has children or represents another word, deleting it would destroy valid words sharing that prefix.

options.text: Only when the app receives a low memory warning from iOS.
options.explanation: Trie pruning is part of standard deletion logic.

options.text: Red-Black balanced binary tree.
options.explanation: A Red-Black tree is a binary search tree, not a compressed trie.

options.text: Fibonacci min-priority heap.
options.explanation: A Fibonacci heap is a priority queue structure.

options.text: Disjoint set union forest.
options.explanation: Disjoint sets manage connected components, not strings.

options.text: Radix tree or Patricia trie.

questions.prompt: Why should TrieNode be implemented as a class rather than a struct in Swift?

options.text: Reference semantics allow mutating deep child nodes in place without copying parent trees.
options.explanation: Classes provide reference semantics; mutating a deep struct trie triggers recursive copy-on-write overhead.

options.text: Swift structs cannot conform to the standard Equatable protocol in iOS applications.
options.explanation: Structs can conform to Equatable without restriction.

options.text: Classes execute on the graphics processing unit automatically without thread dispatch.
options.explanation: Classes execute on standard CPU threads.

options.text: Structs in Swift cannot contain Dictionary properties or any nested reference types.
options.explanation: Structs frequently store Dictionary values in Swift.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain why a trie is superior to a hash set for autocomplete prefix lookups. Mention the time complexity of both approaches.

rubric.criterion: Explains that a hash set requires scanning all N words taking O(N * L) time to find prefix matches
Explains that a trie reaches the prefix node in O(P) time independent of dictionary size N
Notes that common prefixes share storage in a trie

questions.modelAnswer: A hash set cannot perform prefix lookups directly because hash codes scramble string structures. Finding words starting with a prefix in a hash set requires scanning all N entries in O(N * L) time. A trie walks down prefix characters directly in O(P) time, completely independent of the dictionary size.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, describe the difference between the search and startsWith operations on a trie. Give an example showing when their results differ.

rubric.criterion: Explains that search requires isEndOfWord to be true on the target node
Explains that startsWith only requires that the character path exists in the trie
Provides a clear concrete example (such as app when only apple is stored)

questions.modelAnswer: The search operation returns true only if every character exists and the final node has isEndOfWord set to true. The startsWith operation returns true as soon as the full prefix path exists, regardless of the isEndOfWord flag. For example, if only apple is inserted, startsWith(app) returns true while search(app) returns false.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain why TrieNode should be a class rather than a struct in Swift. Discuss memory mutation and tree traversal.

rubric.criterion: Explains that classes have reference semantics allowing in-place mutation of child nodes
Explains that structs have value semantics which trigger recursive copy-on-write during tree updates
Mentions that reference pointers allow multiple paths or parent references without full copies

questions.modelAnswer: TrieNode must be a class because classes provide reference semantics in Swift. When inserting characters down a tree path, reference semantics allow modifying child nodes directly in place. If TrieNode were a struct, mutating a child would trigger copy-on-write across parent nodes, creating significant memory allocation overhead.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain how word deletion works in a trie. State when child nodes can be pruned safely.

rubric.criterion: Explains unsetting the isEndOfWord flag at the target word node
States pruning condition: node can be deleted only if it has no children and isEndOfWord is false
Mentions bottom-up recursive pruning so shared prefixes are preserved

questions.modelAnswer: To delete a word, traverse recursively to the final character node and set isEndOfWord to false. As recursion unwinds, check if the current node has any other children and whether its isEndOfWord flag is false. If it has no children and is not the end of another word, prune the node safely to reclaim memory.

rubric.criterion: Describes storing precomputed top suggestions or frequency scores on prefix nodes
Explains that precomputing avoids deep DFS subtree traversals during live keystrokes
Mentions keeping operations off the main thread or debouncing rapid user input

questions.modelAnswer: To respond within a 16-millisecond frame budget, each trie node can store a precomputed array of top completion strings. When the user types a character, the search jumps directly to the matching node and returns suggestions in O(P) time without deep subtree traversal. In addition, keystrokes can be debounced and queried on a background queue.
